opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd be careful about generalizing too much. Everything I say comes from one position: a faculty member at a particular university, in a particular field, at a particular moment when AI is changing very fast. That's a narrow window, so I try not to present my views as universal rules.

I think some things do carry over. Picking problems you actually care about rather than chasing whatever is hot, being willing to work on things that look unfashionable, spending real time understanding *why* something works instead of just pushing a benchmark number. Those feel fairly durable to me, whether you're in academia or industry, in vision or language or something else entirely.

But a lot of it really depends on context. At NYU I've had a lot of freedom. I can work with students on long-horizon questions, and I'm surrounded by people like Yann and others who encourage thinking about fundamentals. Not everyone has that. If you're a student in a lab with very different resources, or a researcher at a company with product pressure, the right strategy might look quite different. Compute is a good example. Academia can't compete head-on with big industry labs on scale, so the way I think about which problems are worth doing is partly shaped by that constraint. Someone sitting on ten thousand GPUs should probably think differently.

So I'd say take the spirit of it, not the specifics. The principles about curiosity, taste, and honesty in research are probably fairly general. The tactical choices, like what to work on, how to collaborate, and when to go to industry, are much more personal and situational. I'd rather people hear my experience as one data point and then figure out what fits their own situation, instead of treating it as a recipe.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls his perspective a “narrow window” and “one data point,” and explains that researchers’ contexts and resources differ. This communicates that his NYU experience does not represent the broader diversity of research.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair question, and I try to be honest with myself about it. A lot of what I believe about research comes from a fairly specific path: I did my PhD at UC San Diego, then spent several years at Facebook AI Research, and now I'm at NYU. So my views are shaped by having been inside a big industrial lab during a period when compute and data were growing very quickly, and then moving back to a university where you have to think much harder about what you can actually do with limited resources.

I don't think the specifics transfer universally. If you're a student at a smaller school without access to large GPU clusters, or if you're working in a company where the incentives are about shipping products rather than publishing, the day-to-day calculus is very different. I'd be a little suspicious of anyone, including myself, who claims their research philosophy applies to everyone.

But I do think a few things generalize. One is that the most valuable work tends to come from asking a simple question clearly rather than from stacking complexity on top of complexity. ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, the diffusion transformer work, these all started with "what happens if we just do the simplest version of this and look carefully at the result." That instinct doesn't require a big lab. If anything, it's easier to protect when you have fewer resources, because you can't afford to brute force.

Another is that taste matters more than people admit, and taste is something you develop by reading a lot, reimplementing things, and being willing to be wrong in public. That's available to anyone.

And the third is something I say to my students a lot: don't optimize for what the field rewards this quarter. The field changes too fast. Figure out what you actually find interesting and what you have a genuine edge on, and go deep there. That advice is somewhat independent of where you sit.

So I'd say the principles travel, but the tactics don't. I'd encourage people to listen to how I think about problems and then translate it into their own situation, rather than copying what I did.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Xie’s views as shaped by his specific path and says research circumstances differ across universities and companies, so his experience does not apply universally.

astra-6.text: I think some of the lessons might apply more broadly, but I’d be careful about generalizing from my own experience. NYU is one environment, and the people you work with, the resources you have, and the stage of your career all shape how you approach research. So I’d offer my views as a perspective, rather than a recipe. The useful question is which parts make sense in your own situation.
